back: A plant used for its medicinal, flavouring or pest-repelling properties.
The chemical in a plant (or medicine) that produces its effect.
Its leaves are made into a tea traditionally used for coughs, colds and fevers.
notes: A traditional use, not a proven cure.

back: Applied to minor burns, cuts and skin irritation; added to the drinking water of village chickens.
notes: Swallowing the yellow sap can cause diarrhoea.

back: Leaf or seed extract contains azadirachtin, which repels insects and stops them feeding and growing.
Leaves make a pesticide (rotenoids, very toxic to fish); the plant adds nitrogen to soil.
Cheap, available locally, part of indigenous knowledge, botanical pesticides break down quickly, source of new medicines.
Uncertain dose, side effects and toxicity, lack of testing, may delay proper treatment, over-harvesting.

front: Three medicines developed from plant chemicals
back: Aspirin (willow bark), quinine (cinchona bark), artemisinin (sweet wormwood).

front: Rule for using herbal remedies safely
back: Use them alongside, never instead of, medical care for serious illness; tell the health worker about any herbs taken.
